summary: Trump held a surprise White House briefing on Tuesday with UFC CEO Dana White, where he defended Defense Secretary Hegseth against impeachment articles introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie on the House floor.

Following Massie's introduction of impeachment articles, Hegseth said he was "not worried" about the proceedings. Massie, who lost his primary seat this year, has long feuded with the Trump administration.

When Collins countered that Massie claimed Hegseth carried out "illegal acts," Trump descended into name-calling, calling her a "loser" at CNN. Monday's insult marked at least the fourth personal attack Trump has aimed at Collins this year.

Jake Tapper defended his colleague on social media, stating there is "one person in this exchange whose behavior, hand-picked candidates, and policies were repudiated handily by voters." Tapper's support came after Trump's September attacks on Collins.

This clash occurs amid a broader legal battle between the White House and media outlets including CNN and Politico after the administration attempted to bar them from the White House in September. The legal fight continues to block CNN from pool coverage.
title: Trump says Hegseth should be praised, not impeached

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Waller’s position as strengthening the Fed’s hawkish “falcons,” emphasizing institutional division while de-emphasizing inflation details and the possible 50-basis-point move.

Right-Leaning coverage portrays tightening as an urgent response requiring action “swiftly and forcefully,” stressing concern over the breadth of price increases and conditioning a larger hike on persistent inflation.
Center coverage distinguishes a likely 25-basis-point increase from a possible 50-point move, warns the Fed could “risk its own credibility,” and notes effects on bitcoin and stock futures.
All agree Waller favors at least 25 points, reflecting broader tensions over inflation control versus economic and market risks.
summary: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Tuesday he would support a 0.25% interest-rate hike at the Dec. FOMC meeting, emphasizing the importance of policy follow-through to maintain Fed credibility regardless of upcoming inflation readings.

Waller argued that failing to implement promised hikes would cause Markets to reduce expectations and loosen monetary policy undesirably, adding that higher rates "will be needed, sooner rather than later."

Following the speech, Markets immediately repriced the probability of a Dec. quarter-point hike from 76.3% to 96.3%, per CME Group's FedWatch Tool, while investors expect the Oct Consumer Price Index to show a 0.3% monthly increase.
Bitcoin fell 1.3% to $74,080 as traders reacted to higher borrowing cost prospects, while Nasdaq futures declined 0.4% ahead of the Wall Street open and the Labor Statistics inflation report.

Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee cautioned on Monday that the Fed must prevent the economy from running too hot, noting that "because once it gets overheated, it's extremely painful to get rid of that kind of overheating.
title: Fed Governor Waller sees December hike likely, opens door to possible half-point increase

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames a “controversial” boycott met by pro-Israel supporters, emphasizing police estimates—about 300 protesters versus 200 counterprotesters—and organizers’ claim that the Kristallnacht timing was coincidental.

Right-Leaning coverage instead labels participants “antisemites” or “leftist,” portrays the action as targeting Jewish-owned businesses, and celebrates that it “backfired big time,” invoking Kristallnacht and arrests to intensify moral condemnation.
Center coverage de-emphasizes ideological judgment, highlighting “massive” crowds, skirmishes, and the boycott flyer.

The pivotal divide is whether the event represents anti-Zionist protest or antisemitic targeting; all perspectives nevertheless stress six Jewish-owned eateries, a substantial counterprotest, and confrontation.
summary: On Sunday, a massive crowd of counter-protesters gathered in Rittenhouse Square, Philadelphia, to support Jewish-owned businesses targeted by a bike boycott organized by groups calling the restaurants "Zionist establishments."

A flyer circulating since October 30, 2026, promoted the boycott against six Jewish-owned eateries including Goldie and K'Far Cafe; critics condemned the timing, as the event fell on the 88th anniversary of Kristallnacht, the 1938 Nazi pogrom.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker condemned the targeting as antisemitism, while the businesses, owned by Michael Solomonov's group, faced scrutiny for prior fundraising of more than $100,000 for the Friends of United Hatzalah following the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.

The bike boycott effectively collapsed soon after starting as counter-demonstrators formed lines outside the targeted eateries; Philadelphia Police reported three arrests during the tense event, though no major physical altercations occurred.

Organizers have reportedly teased another event dubbed a "ride of return" slated for November 15, 2026, while community members emphasize the need for ongoing patronage rather than just a one-day surge.
title: Hundreds gather in Philadelphia for Pro-Palestinian demonstration and counterprotest

summary: On Monday, the Crown withdrew all criminal charges against 44 pro-Palestinian protesters arrested during an April 2024 sit-in at a downtown Montreal Scotiabank, officially ending the prosecution.
Protesters occupied the branch demanding Scotiabank divest from Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, a move the bank eventually completed, which activists welcomed as a victory.

While 14 individuals previously pleaded guilty to municipal noise bylaw violations and paid $300 fines, defense lawyer Barbara Bedont noted most other protesters resolved their cases through community service.
Defendants challenged the charges under the Charter, arguing police violated their rights, and filed a formal complaint against the presiding judge alleging bias and unfair treatment.
Defense counsel Bedont warned that criminalizing peaceful sit-ins threatens the right to protest, suggesting the group's legal strategy likely influenced the Crown's decision to drop charges.
title: No Criminal Charges for Montreal Protesters Arrested at Bank Sit-In

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Trump as bringing Dana White to “defend embattled allies,” implying political damage control, while right-leaning accounts portray the appearance as Trump having “a little fun,” with White’s “zero political aspirations” definitively ending staffing speculation.
Center coverage emphasizes a “surprise” or “bedlam”-filled briefing and adds Trump’s “combative” response to an electoral defeat.

The pivotal divide is whether White’s podium appearance signals strategic defense, playful theater, or disorder; right-leaning details about a Trump-Biden fight and Pete Rose pardon reinforce entertainment framing.
All perspectives agree White appeared, answered questions, and declined the role, reflecting broader tensions over Trump’s political style and media spectacle.
summary: On Monday, President Donald Trump joked about appointing UFC CEO Dana White as press secretary during a Washington event, with the position vacant since Katie Zacharia and Karoline Leavitt departed.
Truth Social posts ignited widespread speculation about White's appointment after Trump's announcement calling him a "violent fighter and warrior" led many to believe the president was serious.
At the podium, White said "the last 24 hours of my life has been insane" and dismissed political aspirations, confirming he is a long-time friend of the president.
Trump clarified on Sunday night he was "having a little fun," saying he sent the post to reporters who "wrote the stories as though I wasn't kidding."
The president then addressed weighty matters, discussing the Iran and Ukraine wars, the possible impeachment of Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, and a spy scandal involving Nvidia boss Jensen Huang.
title: Dana White takes podium at White House press briefing

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Trump’s remarks as inconsistency, using “backtracks” and stressing his shift from calling deportation “too tough” to deeming it “very strong.” Right-leaning coverage instead spotlights a possible retreat toward legal status, amplifying “amnesty,” “betrayal,” and conservative supporters who “seethe,” while emphasizing the White House’s denial and Trump’s claim that farm and hotel workers faced “not even close” the pressure applied to serious offenders.
Center coverage foregrounds the “worst of the worst” and post-midterm backlash.

The dividing line is whether negotiation signals moderation or capitulation; all emphasize Trump’s proposed deal, rejection of amnesty, and tough enforcement, reflecting wider disputes over border control, party loyalty, and humanitarian versus economic priorities.
summary: President Donald Trump pushed back against suggestions that his immigration stance is softening, insisting during a White House press appearance that his administration maintains a "very strong deportation policy".
Fully ruling out any form of legal relief, Trump stated plainly that there is "no amnesty, no, no anything" for undocumented immigrants living in the country.

The remarks came in the wake of comments where Trump acknowledged that mass deportation tactics might have been "too tough" during the midterm elections, alongside questions raised by his promotion of hardline immigration architect Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff.

While maintaining that enforcement remains a core priority, Trump acknowledged that some undocumented individuals have built stable lives, noting that "many of them have good jobs now" and are productive, tax-paying members of society.

Trump reiterated that federal enforcement will continue to target individuals he classified as the "worst of the worst"—such as violent criminals and drug traffickers—while his administration evaluates its next steps.
title: Trump Says Deportation Policy Unchanged, Rules Out Immigration Amnesty

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the case as a threat to “accountability,” warning that the Court could “shield” officers and bar “victims” from remedies, especially amid complaints about “aggressive and sometimes violent” ICE actions.

Right-Leaning coverage instead portrays the 1971 Bivens remedy as “judicial overreach,” emphasizes the roughly $3 million claim after a 2021 Honolulu prison fight, and presents ending lawsuits as institutional restraint.

Center coverage is more measured, stressing justices’ “wary” posture and the possible end of the “Bivens experiment.” All emphasize the medical-care dispute, damages, and potential limits on suits, reflecting a broader divide over civil rights, accountability, and judicial power.
summary: On Monday, the Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Nielsen v. Watanabe, examining whether citizens can sue federal law enforcement officers for damages when constitutional rights are violated.
Kekai Watanabe alleges that prison nurse Francis Nielsen violated his Eighth Amendment rights by refusing medical care after a 2021 gang riot at the Federal Detention Center in Honolulu.
The lawsuit challenges the 1971 Bivens decision, which created a path to sue federal officers for constitutional violations. Attorneys for Nielsen argue the precedent is now obsolete.
Chief Justice John Roberts appeared open to a narrower ruling during Monday's arguments, questioning why the court should not defer to the government's "cautious, incremental" approach.
Experts warn that eliminating Bivens could grant federal officers absolute immunity. With the Accountability for Federal Law Enforcement Act stalled, a decision is expected by June 2027.
title: Supreme Court appears wary of former inmate’s quest for damages over prison medical care

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the decision as a troubling retreat from oversight, using “shun,” “boycott,” “serious human rights violations,” and calls for “accountability,” while highlighting civil-society criticism.

Right-Leaning coverage, unusually critical of the administration, similarly portrays Trump as refusing scrutiny through “snub,” “outrage,” and “refuses to submit,” emphasizing the repeated boycott and the postponed 2026 review.

Center coverage de-emphasizes activist reaction, instead presenting the unprecedented procedural development and the administration’s claim of UN “bias.” The pivotal divide is whether withdrawal signals evasiveness or sovereignty, though all perspectives stress the first complete nonparticipation and the broader conflict over U.S. autonomy versus international human-rights norms.
summary: On Tuesday, the United States became the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the United Nations Human Rights Council.
Citing anti-United States and anti-Israel bias, the Trump administration withdrew from the Council last year, alleging it failed to uphold its own values.

Participation by the country under review is required by the Geneva-based council; without national representatives, the review cannot proceed, and it typically examines all 193 United Nations member states.
Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union, told reporters Monday that the administration is "saying to the world, we don't care about whether you would review us or not."

Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute, warned the walkout could undermine the review system's credibility, noting that if the predominant global power ignores rights norms, the system faces "big trouble.
title: U.S. Skips U.N. Human Rights Review, First Nation to Fully Opt Out

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the investigation as an unresolved child-safety failure, using phrases like “still running” stop signs and questioning whether Waymo ’s recall worked.

Right-Leaning coverage adopts a more bureaucratic “compliance” lens, emphasizing NHTSA’s review of 2,895 vehicles and whether a software update fixed the defect, though “new violations” heightens concern.
Center coverage bridges both, stressing “probe,” “illegally,” and continued violations while detailing flashing lights, stop arms, and the December 2025 recall.
The dividing line is accountability versus regulatory procedure, but all perspectives emphasize alleged post-recall failures and the stakes of autonomous vehicles near school buses.
summary: On Monday, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a recall query into 2,895 Waymo vehicles operated by Alphabet, examining continued traffic safety violations involving the robotaxis failing to yield to stopped school buses.

Waymo issued a voluntary software recall in December 2025 to prevent vehicles from passing school buses with flashing red lights, yet officials are investigating why violations persisted despite the update deployment.

Public schools documented 19 violations in Austin, Texas, including one incident where a driverless car proceeded while a student was actively crossing the street; six additional violations occurred in Atlanta, Georgia.

The NHTSA recall query began on Friday to determine whether the update worked, since "a majority of incidents occurred after the... remedy date," and investigators aim to "identify the causes of the conditions leading to the post-remedy reports."

Separately, the National Transportation Safety Board launched its own investigation into Waymo behavior earlier this year, while the NHTSA opened a probe in January following a collision involving a Waymo vehicle and a child in Santa Monica, California.
title: US opens new probe into Waymo vehicles over school bus safety violations

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Owens as a “far-right conspiracy theorist” spreading “false” claims, emphasizing alleged repetition, broader conspiracies, and the Macrons’ persistence after Delaware jurisdictional limits.

Right-Leaning coverage foregrounds the provocative “a man” or “transgender” allegation and portrays the Tennessee filing as additional legal pressure on a conservative commentator, inviting a censorship or retaliation reading.

Center coverage de-emphasizes ideological combat, stressing the federal venue, procedural continuation, and roughly 409-page complaint, while attributing phrases like “devastating lies.” The dividing line is whether the story centers alleged misinformation or litigation against a media figure; all perspectives emphasize defamation proceedings, the Tennessee connection, and the identity-related dispute.
summary: French President Emmanuel Macron and First Lady Brigitte Macron filed a personal federal defamation lawsuit against podcaster Candace Owens in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee.

The fresh filing comes on the heels of an October 27 ruling by a Delaware superior court judge, who dismissed personal claims against Owens in an earlier July 2025 lawsuit due to a lack of personal jurisdiction, ruling that the court only had authority over her registered business entities.

The sprawling 409-page complaint accuses Owens of repeatedly publishing defamatory claims regarding Brigitte Macron's identity and the couple's marital history, noting that she continued and expanded upon the allegations even after the initial litigation was launched.

Legal representatives for the Macrons argue that Tennessee is the appropriate venue because Owens resides in Nashville and allegedly produced and disseminated the contested material from within the state.
The couple is demanding a jury trial alongside actual, presumed, and punitive damages, as well as a permanent injunction barring Owens from republishing statements deemed defamatory by the court.
title: French President Emmanuel Macron, Wife Sue Candace Owens in Nashville

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds contract workers, “toxic gas,” and possible “safety lapses,” casting the deaths during wastewater-tank maintenance as a labor and corporate-accountability failure.

Right-Leaning coverage widens the frame: it raises possible drowning in a nano-filtration tank, stresses safety concerns, Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board and police inquiries, and calls it the “latest supply chain incident,” while portraying India as a “critical manufacturing base”; “tragedy has struck an Apple factory” adds dramatic corporate association.

Center coverage uses cautious attribution—“suspected asphyxiation”—and calls the event a “tragedy.” All agree three outsourced workers died at Tata’s Apple-linked facility and investigations followed, revealing tensions over regulation, accountability, and India’s manufacturing expansion.
summary: On Monday, three contract workers died of asphyxiation while performing cleaning and maintenance work inside a nano-filtration feed tank at a Tata Electronics Private Limited facility near Uddanapalli.
While cleaning the Effluent Treatment Plant , one worker fainted after inhaling toxic gas, and two other employees subsequently collapsed while attempting to provide immediate assistance.
The victims were identified as B. Akmal and M. Sarathi Kumar from Dharmapuri, and Kaveri from Hosur, all of whom were employed by a contractor engaged by Nalco.

Krishnagiri District Collector Dinesh Kumar initiated an investigation into potential industrial safety lapses, while the victims' bodies were transferred to the Government Krishnagiri Medical College Hospital for postmortem examinations.

Preliminary police inquiries indicate the workers suffered from gas exposure, though final reports will confirm the exact cause while local officials continue monitoring the situation around the facility.
title: Three workers die at Tata's India iPhone parts factory in latest safety incident: Report
